caption:
Nobody pays your super when you're the boss. That's also one of the biggest legal levers you have.

Sole traders can make personal super contributions and claim them as a tax deduction. On $120K profit in 2026–27, putting $20K into super cuts tax and Medicare by $6,400; the fund pays $3,000 in contributions tax; about $3,400 more stays yours.

The rules: the 2026–27 concessional cap is $32,500, unused cap from up to 5 past years can carry forward if your super balance was under $500K, and you must give your fund a notice of intent and get its acknowledgement before you lodge. The catch: the money is locked away, the cash leaves the business now, and over $250K Division 293 adds 15%.

Big contribution? Worth running past a registered adviser first.

Save this for June.

General info only, not personal advice.

figures_checked: 2026-27 resident rates + 2% Medicare (ATO Tax rates – Australian residents, checked 1 Nov 2026); $120K = $26,520 + $2,400, $100K = $20,520 + $2,000

Personal deductible contributions: notice of intent by earlier of lodgment or end of next income year, acknowledgement before claiming, taxed 15%, count to concessional cap; work test 67-74 (ATO Personal super contributions, checked 1 Nov 2026)
Concessional cap 2026-27 $32,500; carry-forward 5 years, TSB < $500,000 (ATO, checked 1 Nov 2026)
